hook.line: When you have thought about a problem for hours and nothing comes, English says you racked your brain. Spanish says you broke your head, and it sounds just as dramatic as it feels.
hook.es: Me rompí la cabeza tratando de entenderlo.
hook.en: I racked my brains trying to understand it.

examples.en: I racked my brains trying to understand it.

rule:
*Romperse la cabeza* (or *quebrarse la cabeza*, very common in Latin America) is to think hard about something without an easy answer.

It is reflexive: *me, te, se, nos* match the person thinking. And it says *la cabeza*, not *mi cabeza*, because the pronoun already says whose head: *me rompí la cabeza*.

What you were thinking about follows with *tratando de* + verb, *pensando en*, *buscando*: *Me rompí la cabeza pensando en una solución*.

To tell someone not to worry about it: *No te rompas la cabeza*.
smallPrint: Teachers call *la cabeza* here a possessive dative: the reflexive pronoun shows the owner, so the article replaces *mi*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *rompí* or *rompió* and type the sentence about yourself: *Me ___ la cabeza tratando de entenderlo.*
yourTurn.answer: Me rompí la cabeza tratando de entenderlo.
yourTurn.why: *Me* and the ending *-í* both say it is you.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I racked my brains thinking of a solution.
yourTurn.answer: Me quebré la cabeza pensando en una solución.
accept: Me rompí la cabeza pensando en una solución.
yourTurn.why: *Me quebré* is "I broke" in the past, with *la cabeza*, not *mi cabeza*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: Don't rack your brains, I'll sort it out. (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: No te rompas la cabeza, yo lo arreglo.
accept: No te quiebres la cabeza, yo lo arreglo.
yourTurn.why: A negative command to a friend swaps the vowel: *-es* for *-ar* verbs, *-as* for *-er* and *-ir* ones. *Romper* gives *rompas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: We racked our brains all night.
yourTurn.answer: Nos rompimos la cabeza toda la noche.
accept: Nos quebramos la cabeza toda la noche.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about Tomás: *Me rompí la cabeza pensando en la carta.* Say: Tomás racked his brains thinking about the letter.
yourTurn.answer: Tomás se rompió la cabeza pensando en la carta.
accept: Se rompió la cabeza pensando en la carta.
yourTurn.why: *Se rompió* is for "he" in the past.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it a question to a friend: *Me rompí la cabeza con la carta.* Say: Did you rack your brains over the letter? (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: ¿Te rompiste la cabeza con la carta?
yourTurn.why: *Te rompiste* is the "you" past, with the question marks added.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: She racked her brains trying to remember his name.
yourTurn.answer: Se rompió la cabeza tratando de recordar su nombre.
accept: Ella se rompió la cabeza tratando de recordar su nombre.
yourTurn.why: *Tratando de* + verb says what the effort was for.

pitfalls.wrong: Rompí mi cabeza tratando de entenderlo.
pitfalls.right: Me rompí la cabeza tratando de entenderlo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. Spanish puts the owner in the pronoun *me*, so the head becomes *la cabeza*.

pitfalls.wrong: Me rompí la cabeza a entenderlo.
pitfalls.right: Me rompí la cabeza tratando de entenderlo.
pitfalls.why: Almost. English "trying to" becomes *tratando de* or *pensando en*.
Almost. A negative command to a friend swaps the vowel: *romper* gives *rompas*, not *rompes*.

personal: What problem has made you rack your brains lately? Say it with *Me rompí la cabeza pensando en…*.
